items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Oscar hated Bud Powell and so did Don and all the rest of them. They didn’t like the way he played at all. But Monk was the biggest, so he said, “Let him sit in,” and he’d stand up.

ctx.x: I believe that. So, back to Charlie Parker. How did that occur? How did you meet him? Where did you meet him?

My meeting him – I was in University of Toledo law school, playing drums and singing every night with a local trio. He came to town. I was a star in Toledo. When we got off, we went to the dance. It was a breakfast dance, so they were still playing. It was Bird and – Kenny Dorham had just replaced Miles Davis. It was Tommy Potter on bass, Max Roach on drums, and Al Haig on piano, who was red-headed, a white piano player. That was – that caused a lot of attention. Everybody – “Look at that. He’s got a white piano…

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And Roy Haynes was on drums, Curly Russell was on bass, and Bud Powell was on piano.

ctx.x: With this long goatee. That’s the way Gerry had this long, red beard and a shock of red hair. And jeans, no socks and tennis shoes. That was how he was dressed on the bandstand. Well those guys were spending all their money on heroin. They were shooting up all day every day. And he was living uptown with Bird at that time. And Roy Haynes was on drums, Curly Russell was on bass, and Bud Powell was on piano. So they were playing “The Song Is You,” the song that I scatted with him as I went by. And as I © Hamilton…

walked past the bandstand, now it had been two years and four months since I had seen him for about nine minutes on this bandstand in Toledo, which is the heart of nowhere. And as I walked past the bandstand, he’s playing [scats], “hey Jon, how you doin’ man, you want to sing some?” I almost fainted. It took my breath away. I said good Lord, who the hell is that?
